Beállítom Augusztus végéig megérkezhet az első benzinszállítmány Törökországból Oroszországba – írta vasárnap a Kommerszant című lap az S&P Global Commodities at Sea (CAS) adataira hivatkozva. Az elemzők szerint a Mersin kikötőből elindult Wendrix elnevezésű, MR osztályú 25-50 ezer tonna kapacitású tartályhajó szállítmánya 200 ezer hordó benzin. A VesselFinder adatai szerint a hajó az egyik balti-tengeri kikötőbe tart. Azt, hogy hol gyártották a tartályhajóra rakodott üzemanyagot, nem ismeretes. Ez lesz a július óta ismertté vált ötödik importált benzinszállítmány. A CAS és a Kpler adatai szerint az elmúlt hónapban Oroszország három olyan hajót fogadott, amelyet az egyiptomi partok közelében, hajóról hajóra történő átrakodással töltöttek meg az indiai Vadinar terminálról érkezett üzemanyaggal. Egy további, ismeretlen eredetű benzinszállítmány Marokkóból érkezett, amelynek egyetlen olajfinomítóját 2015-ben bezárták – emlékeztetett az S&P Global. Az elemzők a július vége óta Oroszországba érkezett tengeri benzinszállítások teljes mennyiségét több mint 1 millió hordóra becsülik. Alekszandr Novak miniszterelnök-helyettes szerdán arról számolt be, hogy több olajfinomító újra működésbe lépett, és hogy Moszkva az ellátás javulására számít. Novak szombaton az Interfaxnak elmondta, hogy hiány kizárólag benzinből van az olajfinomítókat ért ukrán dróntámadások következtében, dízelüzemanyagból és kerozinból elegendő mennyiség áll rendelkezésre. https://www.dw.com/en/gaza-at-least-21-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mhqf The search for survivors is ongoing but hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery Image: Mahmoud Issa/REUTERS Advertisement At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble. On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave . "We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found. "My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home." The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues. Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse "The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands." With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory. "There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter." According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents. "Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory. "No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he added. Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave. Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians. More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, said the debate around immigration had become ‘increasingly depressing and toxic’. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, said the debate around immigration had become ‘increasingly depressing and toxic’. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Miatta Fahnbulleh Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’ In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UK Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh , appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration. Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views. In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents. The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers. The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes. Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”. Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month , she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”. “I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added . With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions. “I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said. “I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.” In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.” She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion. “We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.” Explore more on these topics Miatta Fahnbulleh Immigration and asylum Shabana Mahmood news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: A large crowd of local young people and tourists gathers in Europe Square in central Batumi, Georgia, to watch the 2026 World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. Photograph: Alessandro Gandolfi Citizens want greater democracy, while tourists seek out Soviet-era nostalgia, but could Russia’s war on Ukraine be the ultimate decider of country’s fate? Europe live – latest updates By Alessandro Gandolfi Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n the heart of Tbilisi’s Armenian quarter, Avlabari Square is where crowds gather for the “Saturday March”. Every weekend, protesters head towards the Bridge of Love, reach Freedom Square and march towards parliament, chanting slogans against Irakli Kobakhidze’s government. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators in Tblisi take part in the Saturday March, when pro-European parties and movements march through the historic centre to protest against the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which critics accuse of being pro-Russian. View image in fullscreen For years, the target has been the same: Georgian Dream, the ultraconservative party in power since 2012, accused of growing authoritarianism and, through its decision to suspend EU accession talks, moving the country closer to Moscow again. Georgia was granted EU candidate status in 2023. Monday marks two years since the contested parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024 that ignited the political crisis. Protests began two days later and peaked on 28 November, when the government announced it would not put the opening of EU negotiations on its agenda before the end of 2028. View image in fullscreen A woman walks along one of the bridges connecting three Soviet-era towers on Nutsubidze Street in Tblisi. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Two homeless people shelter in the decaying entrance to the Metallurgist sanatorium, an abandoned Soviet-era hotel. Formerly a famous spa town, Tskaltubo hosted 120,000 visitors a year, including Joseph Stalin, who came to enjoy its 22 sanatoriums. After the collapse of the USSR, the area fell into decline and most of the sanatoriums and hotels were abandoned. Today, only a few hundred tourists visit the town’s sole remaining spa centre. View image in fullscreen Books lie scattered across rooms at the Museum of Local Traditions in Tskaltubo, Georgia, where the library is being rebuilt. Georgia is experiencing a curious paradox: while many of its citizen would like the country to be more democratic and form closer ties to Europe , Georgia is attracting growing numbers of tourists drawn to its historic sites, post-Soviet atmosphere and unspoilt landscapes. While the streets of Tbilisi have become the stage for one of the longest protest movements in recent history, in 2025 the country, according to data from the Georgian National Tourism Administration, recorded a high of more than 5.5 million international tourist visits: an 8.4% increase on 2024 and almost 10 times the number (about 560,000) who visited the country 2o years ago. View image in fullscreen A tourist walks through one of the rooms of the Joseph Stalin Museum. The Soviet dictator was born in Gori in 1878, and the museum was established in 1937 near his birthplace. Transformed into a museum glorifying Stalin in 1957, it remained open even after the collapse of the USSR and the 2008 war with Russia . View image in fullscreen Travellers come not only from Europe; many are from the Middle East, and large numbers come from Russia. After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, tens of thousands of Russian citizens relocated to Georgia, bringing money and opening businesses, but also exerting strong pressure on the property market by buying homes across the country. This has fuelled discontent among a population that, mindful of the early 1990s wars against Russian-backed separatists in South Ossetia and Abkhazia, and the brief August 2008 war fought against Moscow, also in South Ossetia, continues to consider Russia an occupying power. View image in fullscreen An abandoned Soviet-era building in Chiatura – one of Georgia’s most important mining towns, where manganese is extracted. The industry faces a severe environmental and economic crisis, which has prompted continuing protests by workers. View image in fullscreen An inhabited Soviet-era building in Chiatura. The mythical land of the Golden Fleece and the Argonauts – the ancient Greeks called the journey to reach it “the longest possible voyage” – is now a republic roughly the size of Ireland, with a population of fewer than 4 million. Georgia emerged from the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. Sandwiched between Russia and Turkey (alongside Armenia and Azerbaijan), it offers a wealth of attractions that draw tourists: quaint mountain villages scattered along the Georgian Military Road, ancient Orthodox churches overlooking rivers and valleys, fascinating post-Soviet cities with a decaying atmosphere, wine with a millennia-old history, a lively “Las Vegas” on the Black Sea (the port of Batumi) and a dynamic, cosmopolitan capital. View image in fullscreen Visitors relax on the pebble beach north of the historic centre in Batumi, with a large container ship heading into the port in the background. Home to numerous casinos and a rapidly growing tourist destination, Batumi is known as the ‘Las Vegas of the Black Sea’ and is also an important commercial port. View image in fullscreen Tbilisi, with its rich underground scene and repurposed industrial spaces, is reminiscent of 1990s Berlin. One of its crown jewels, a true symbol of national independence, is the Rustaveli theatre, renovated 20 years ago by the billionaire who founded Georgian Dream in 2012: Bidzina Ivanishvili. Now in his 70s, Ivanishvili served as Georgian prime minister between 2012 and 2013 and made his fortune in Russia during the 1990s after the Soviet collapse. View image in fullscreen People on a train in Tbilisi. Opened in 1966 to facilitate travel in a city that stretches along the river and is built on steep slopes, the metro network was the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union. Today, the metro, which has two lines and 23 stations, carries 400,000 passengers a day. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen A woman takes a selfie overlooking Tbilisi from Mtatsminda Park. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Tourists take photos near the Leghvtakhevi waterfall in Tbilisi, while others capture the scenery from the funicular leading to Mtatsminda Park. View image in fullscreen Georgians attend a concert at Mtatsminda Park. Founded in the 1930s, the park stands 770 metres above sea level and features restaurants, a rollercoaster, a concert venue, and a large ferris wheel visible from much of Tbilisi. Today, the relationship between Georgia and Russia is built on a contradiction that is difficult to resolve. After the 2008 conflict and the consolidation of Russian military control over Abkhazia and South Ossetia (regions accounting for approximately 20% of Georgian territory), diplomatic relations between the countries were severed. View image in fullscreen Yet economically, Moscow remains a partner that is difficult to replace: trade, tourism, remittances and Russian capital, along with energy imports, prop up Tbilisi’s economy, which, despite strong growth – GDP rose by 7.5% in 2025, marking five consecutive years of expansion – continues to be affected by unemployment, low wages, widespread poverty and, in many rural areas, depopulation. But Georgia’s predicament extends beyond its domestic political crisis, reflecting wider geopolitical tensions. View image in fullscreen A woman picks flowers in the hills surrounding Gergeti Trinity church, beneath Mount Kazbek. View image in fullscreen Worshippers leave Gergeti Trinity church after mass on 16 July. The day marks the Gergetoba festival, also known as the Day of Spiritual Love. Relations with Brussels have deteriorated recently; the EU has criticised the Georgian government’s record on the rule of law and political repression. And many believe a strengthening of Moscow in the Ukraine war could significantly increase its ability to exert pressure on the Caucasus. Both of which make the question inevitable: does the future of a vulnerable Georgia – internationally isolated and with limited domestic support – also hinge on the fate of Ukraine?
